title: Orientation and toolkit
why: Every later module assumes you can use a terminal, version your work with git, debug C, rebuild a Python environment, read papers and, above all, measure performance honestly. From Module 4 to the end, almost every project ends in a speed claim, so this module has you build the small benchmark tool you will use for all of them. The repo you create here, `kiln`, holds every module's work.

steps.title: Missing Semester: get comfortable in the shell
steps.detail: Use the terminal on macOS or Linux. On Windows, set up WSL2 first (next step) and work inside it. Do the exercises at the bottom of the page.

steps.title: Set up a Unix-like environment (macOS, Linux or Windows)
steps.detail: macOS: run `xcode-select --install` for clang, make, git and lldb, then install Homebrew for everything else. Linux: install the build tools with your package manager, e.g. `sudo apt install build-essential clang gdb git` (Debian/Ubuntu) or `sudo dnf install gcc clang gdb git make` (Fedora). Windows: run `wsl --install` (this page), then follow the Linux line inside WSL and keep your course files under `~/` in the Linux filesystem, not `/mnt/c`, or builds will be slow.

steps.title: Missing Semester: the command-line environment
steps.detail: Pipes, environment variables, job control and dotfiles. Pay attention to environment variables: the project's experiment changes nothing but the environment and measures the effect.

steps.title: Missing Semester: set up your editor and tools
steps.detail: You do not need to switch editors. Set up your main editor with clangd (C) and a Python language server, and learn enough Vim to edit a file over ssh.

steps.title: Missing Semester: how Git works
steps.detail: Understand the data model (blobs, trees, commits, refs) rather than memorizing commands.

steps.title: Learn Git Branching: interactive Git practice in the browser
steps.detail: Do the Introduction Sequence on the Main tab and the first two levels on the Remote tab. Interactive drills for commit, branch, merge, rebase and remotes. Then use one branch per module and tag each finished module.

steps.title: Missing Semester: debugging and profiling
steps.detail: printf debugging, debuggers, sanitizers and profilers. Modules 1-4 use all of these.

steps.title: Learn to use a debugger (LLDB on Mac, GDB on Linux)
steps.detail: Make sure clang (or gcc) and make work. Compile a buggy program with `-g -O0 -fsanitize=address`, then set a breakpoint, step, print a variable and get a backtrace. Use lldb on macOS (it ships with the Command Line Tools) and gdb on Linux or WSL (https://www.gnu.org/software/gdb/documentation/); the commands map almost one to one.

steps.title: Makefile Tutorial: write a small Makefile
steps.detail: Read Getting Started, Targets, Variables and Phony targets. That is enough for the project's `make test` and `make bench` targets.

steps.title: Set up Python environments with uv
steps.detail: Create one project environment for kiln with numpy, matplotlib and pytest (PyTorch comes later, in Module 7). Commit `uv.lock`. The project's `kbench.py` and its tests run in this environment.

steps.title: Python argparse tutorial: give your script command-line options
steps.detail: Read up to 'Short options'. kbench needs `-n`, `--warmup` and everything after `--` as the command (`nargs=argparse.REMAINDER`). For running that command and capturing its output, read the `subprocess.run` section of https://docs.python.org/3/library/subprocess.html.

steps.title: pytest: write and run your first tests
steps.detail: Read the whole page (about 15 minutes). The project's `tests/test_kbench.py` uses plain `assert` and, for the CSV test, the `tmp_path` fixture shown there.

steps.title: Matplotlib quick start: make your first plot
steps.detail: Read up to 'Styling Artists'. You need one line plot with error bars (`ax.errorbar`), axis labels and `fig.savefig`.

steps.title: S. Keshav, How to Read a Paper
steps.detail: A short paper. Use the three-pass method on each paper in this course and keep a one-paragraph summary per paper in your repo.

steps.title: Mytkowicz et al., Producing Wrong Data Without Doing Anything Obviously Wrong!
steps.detail: The ASPLOS 2009 paper showing that the size of your environment variables and the link order can change a benchmark's speed enough to flip a conclusion. Read sections 1-4; the project asks you to reproduce the environment-size effect.

steps.title: LLVM benchmarking tips: how to get stable timings
steps.detail: A short page from the LLVM developers on reducing noise: fixed CPU frequency, pinning to a core, quiet machine. Apply what your OS allows and record what you could not control.

steps.title: hyperfine: a command-line benchmarking tool
steps.detail: Install it (`brew install hyperfine` on macOS, `sudo apt install hyperfine` on Debian/Ubuntu) and time any command with `hyperfine --warmup 3 'cmd'`. Your own tool in the project does the same job; use hyperfine to check its numbers.

steps.title: GitHub Actions quickstart: run checks on every push
steps.detail: Make the demo workflow run once, then write your own `ci.yml`. To install uv and run pytest in CI, follow https://docs.astral.sh/uv/guides/integration/github/.

steps.title: Start a learning log (Julia Evans, write a brag document)
steps.detail: Keep `LOG.md` in kiln with one dated entry per session: what you did, what confused you, what you will do next. This is your only log; write one short public post per module from it. The easiest place to publish is GitHub Pages (quickstart: https://docs.github.com/en/pages/quickstart).

project.title: kiln v0.0: the repo and a benchmark tool you will use all course
project.brief: kiln is the one repo for this whole course. It grows into a small ML library with its own compiler: tensors in Module 1, autograd in Module 6, a graph IR in Module 8, and from Module 19 the course compiler (`./compile`) becomes its backend. Module exercises and skill projects go in `labs/NN-name/` inside the same repo. In this module you set it up and build `kbench`, a small timing tool, then use it to reproduce a real result: changing only the size of the environment can change how fast a program runs.
steps: Create a public GitHub repo named `kiln` with these files and folders: `README.md`, `LICENSE` (MIT is fine), `LOG.md`, `Makefile`, `bench/`, `labs/00-setup/`, `tests/`, and the `pyproject.toml` and `uv.lock` from the uv step.

In `labs/00-setup/`, write `sum.c`: fill an array of 10 million ints with small values (for example `i % 100`), add them into a `long long` total (an `int` total would overflow), and print it. Make it take about 0.1-0.5 s; if it is faster, repeat the loop. In the Makefile add two targets: `make sum` builds `./sum` with `-O2` for timing, and `make test` builds a separate `./sum_asan` with `-g -fsanitize=address,undefined`, runs it and checks the printed total.

Write `bench/kbench.py`. Running `python bench/kbench.py -n 20 --warmup 3 -- ./sum` should run the command 3 times without timing it, then 20 times timing each run with `time.perf_counter()` around `subprocess.run`, and append one row to `results.csv`. Add a `--label` option whose text is stored in the row, so you can tell runs apart later. The row holds: the command, number of runs, median, min, max, the interquartile range (the spread of the middle half of the runs: `statistics.quantiles(times, n=4)` gives the quartiles), the git commit (`git rev-parse --short HEAD`), the compiler version (first line of `cc --version`), the OS (`platform.platform()`) and the CPU model (`platform.processor()`, or `sysctl -n machdep.cpu.brand_string` on macOS, `/proc/cpuinfo` on Linux). Then add `make bench`, which builds `./sum` and runs kbench on it; let `make bench RUNS=3` set `-n` so CI can run a quick version.

Write `tests/test_kbench.py` with pytest. Put the median and interquartile-range math in plain functions so you can test them on fixed lists such as `[1, 2, 3, 4, 100]`, and check that one run writes a CSV row with every column filled.
Time the same `./sum` with hyperfine (`hyperfine --warmup 3 -N ./sum`). The two medians should agree within a few percent; if not, find out why. Note both numbers in `labs/00-setup/README.md`.

The experiment: in a bash loop, `for N in $(seq 0 64 4096)`, run `python bench/kbench.py -n 20 --warmup 3 --label $N -- env "PAD=$(head -c $N /dev/zero | tr '\0' x)" ./sum`. Each run adds a dummy environment variable of N x's; keep the quotes, or the shell may mangle it. That is 65 sizes and takes about 10 minutes. Then write a short Python script that reads `results.csv`, takes the rows with these labels, and plots median time (min and max as error bars) against N into `labs/00-setup/env_size.png`.

Write about one page in `labs/00-setup/README.md`: what you measured, the plot, whether the change across N is bigger than the run-to-run spread, and what you could not control (other apps, laptop power mode, CPU frequency). The paper saw its effect with variables on the stack; if you see nothing, say so and show the noise. An honest null result passes.

Add `.github/workflows/ci.yml` (start from the GitHub Actions C starter workflow in Go deeper) that on every push installs uv, then runs `make test`, `uv run pytest`, and `make bench RUNS=3` as a quick check that the tool still works. Do not trust timings from CI machines.
Publish one short post (500-1000 words) on GitHub Pages, a blog or similar: what kiln will become, your study schedule, and your environment-size result with the plot. Link it from the README.
deliverables: public `kiln` repo with the layout above, all green in GitHub Actions
`bench/kbench.py` with its pytest, checked against hyperfine
`labs/00-setup/README.md` with the environment-size plot and write-up
`LOG.md` with at least 3 dated entries, and one published post linked from the README

rubric.solid: CI is green; kbench reports median, min, max and interquartile range and records the environment; it agrees with hyperfine; the plot exists and the write-up compares the effect to the noise honestly.
rubric.exceptional: Also pins the process to one core and fixes the CPU frequency where the OS allows (Linux `taskset` and `cpupower`), repeats the experiment with link order changed (the paper's second effect), and gives a bootstrap confidence interval for each median.

project.title: kiln v0.1: an arena-allocated tensor core in C
project.brief: Start kiln with a small C library, `tcore`, that stores N-dimensional float32 tensors (shape, strides, offset, data) in an arena allocator, with elementwise add and mul, a naive matmul and a C test suite. Every later kiln version builds on it, and the C your compiler generates in Part III will link against it. Benchmark creating and freeing `10^4`, `10^5` and `10^6` tensors of 16, 256 and 4096 floats with the arena vs `malloc/free`, and explain the difference. Time each case with your `kbench` tool from Module 0.
deliverables: repo with `tcore.h/tcore.c`, a Makefile, and tests that run clean under ASan, UBSan and valgrind
README with a table and plot of allocation throughput (arena vs `malloc`) across tensor counts and sizes
a 600–1200 word write-up explaining your memory layout, ownership rules, and why arenas suit compiler-generated code

project.title: tcore++: a modern C++ tensor wrapper with Python bindings
project.brief: Wrap your kiln v0.1 C core in a header-only C++20 library. `Tensor<T>` owns its storage through RAII, is movable but not implicitly copyable, supports strided views that share storage, and applies elementwise ops passed as lambdas, with `add` and `mul` that call into `tcore` for `float`. Build it with CMake, test it with GoogleTest, benchmark it with Google Benchmark against the raw C calls, and expose it to Python with nanobind so NumPy can read a tensor without copying.
